title: Financial statements
overview: Financial statements communicate performance over a period and financial position at a date. At A2 you must interpret the statement of profit or loss and statement of financial position, understand relationships between them, and know inventory valuation using net realisable value and straight-line depreciation.
syllabusPoints: Explain and interpret the statement of profit or loss and effects of changes on its figures.
Explain and interpret the statement of financial position and links with profit data.
Explain inventory-valuation difficulty and net realisable value.
Calculate/explain straight-line depreciation and its effect on profit and asset values.

definitions.definition: Expected selling value of inventory less the costs necessary to complete/sell it.
Allocation of a non-current asset's depreciable amount over its useful life.
Profits retained in the business rather than distributed to owners.

sections.title: Statement of profit or loss
content: Shows performance over a period. Typical flow: revenue -> cost of sales -> gross profit -> operating expenses -> profit from operations -> finance/tax/other items -> profit for the year. Trace a change through every affected subtotal rather than discussing one line only.

sections.title: Statement of financial position
content: A snapshot at a specific date showing non-current assets, current assets, current liabilities, net current assets, non-current liabilities and equity/reserves. It indicates resources controlled and financing obligations.

sections.title: How the statements connect
content: Retained profit can increase equity/reserves. Depreciation reduces profit and reduces the carrying value of non-current assets. Inventory valuation affects both current assets and cost of sales/profit. The statements therefore must be analysed together.

sections.title: Inventory valuation and NRV
content: Inventory may become damaged, obsolete or fall in selling price. Reporting it above what can be recovered overstates assets and potentially profit. NRV reflects expected recoverable amount after costs needed to complete/sell.

sections.title: Straight-line depreciation
content: The same depreciation expense is charged each year across useful life. It reduces reported profit and the carrying amount of the asset but is not itself a current-year cash payment.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Annual depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life

sections.title: Using statements strategically
content: Statements provide evidence of profitability, liquidity, asset use and financing but are mainly historical. Managers/investors should combine them with ratios, cash-flow forecasts and non-financial information.

analysisChains.title: Higher depreciation expense
steps: Cash does not leave the business at the point depreciation is charged
analysisChains.evaluation: Depreciation methods are accounting estimates, so comparisons require consistent policies and attention to asset age.

examTips: If a transaction/change affects both statements, explain both effects.
Depreciation is an expense/allocation, not a cash outflow in the year it is charged.
commonMistakes: Confusing gross profit and operating profit.
Putting non-current liabilities into current liabilities.
Saying depreciation creates cash for replacement.
